p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Inflation is often described as a tax that no legislature votes for, and like many taxes it does not fall evenly. A salaried professional whose income is linked to an index, or a household with savings in property and shares, may find that rising prices are largely offset by rising wages or asset values. A daily-wage labourer enjoys no such protection. His earnings are fixed by bargaining that lags behind the market, and a far larger share of what he spends goes on food and fuel, the very items whose prices are most volatile. When the cost of pulses or cooking oil rises sharply, a wealthier family economises on luxuries; a poor family cuts the protein from its children's meals.

For this reason, central banks that hold inflation low and stable are performing a service to the poor, even when their decisions are criticised for slowing growth. Yet monetary policy has limits. A spike in food prices caused by a failed monsoon or a disruption of supply cannot be cured by raising interest rates, which act slowly and mostly on demand. Such shocks call for different instruments: well-managed buffer stocks, efficient public distribution and investment in storage and transport that reduce waste between farm and market. Price stability, in short, is a shared responsibility of the bank and the government.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The distinction between medicines and sensual drugs is simple. Sensual drugs are those that the body has no need for, but that give the user a strong sense of pleasure. Sensual drugs activate the brain’s pleasure centres directly or activate them through chemical mimicry. The brain governs sensations, moods, thoughts and actions, not by a magical process but by an incredibly complex series of chemically regulated controls. These are easily upset by sensual drugs. This disturbance is apparent in the effects of the sensual drugs on the mechanism that controls pleasure and satisfaction. A drug user’s craving for the brain’s pleasure reflexes seems to be weakened by artificial stimulation. Information from the senses still reaches the brain, but the brain is unable to evaluate and interpret it as pleasure. In contrast, naturally attained pleasures enlarge the sense of satisfaction and can be repeated indefinitely.

questions.q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
opts: the advantages of investing in property and shares.
the reasons legislatures vote for new taxes.
how rising interest rates cure every kind of price rise.
the uneven burden of inflation on the poor and the combined measures needed to control it.
questions.why: Main idea: inflation 'does not fall evenly', and 'Price stability... is a shared responsibility of the bank and the government'.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, does inflation hurt daily-wage labourers more?
opts: Their wages are linked to a price index.
They hold most of their savings in shares.
They spend a larger share of income on food and fuel, whose prices are most volatile.
They pay higher income tax than professionals.
questions.why: Detail: 'a far larger share of what he spends goes on food and fuel, the very items whose prices are most volatile'.

questions.q: A sharp rise in vegetable prices after widespread floods would most likely be seen by the author as:
opts: an event that affects rich and poor households equally.
a problem best solved by cutting public distribution.
a supply shock that interest rate increases alone are poorly suited to cure.
proof that the central bank has failed in its duty.
questions.why: Inference: a spike 'caused by a failed monsoon or a disruption of supply cannot be cured by raising interest rates'; it calls for buffer stocks and better distribution.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards central banks is best described as:
opts: appreciative of their role, while recognising its limits.
hostile, blaming them for slowing growth.
uncritically confident that they can solve every price problem.
indifferent to what they do.
questions.why: Tone: they 'are performing a service to the poor', 'Yet monetary policy has limits'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'volatile' means:
opts: liable to change rapidly and unpredictably
fixed by the government
likely to explode or catch fire
rising steadily every year
questions.why: Vocabulary: food and fuel prices are 'most volatile', i.e. they rise sharply and unpredictably.

questions.q: According to the passage, sensual drugs differ from medicines chiefly because
opts: they activate the brain's pleasure centres
the body has no need for them
they upset the brain's controls
they are expensive
questions.why: Definition in the second sentence: drugs 'the body has no need for'. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Legal Officer), Sep 2023.

questions.q: Which phrase does NOT describe how sensual drugs work, according to the passage?
opts: giving a strong sense of pleasure
chemical mimicry
a magical process
artificial stimulation
questions.why: The passage says the brain works 'not by a magical process'. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Legal Officer), Sep 2023.

questions.q: Why does a drug user stop experiencing ordinary sensations as pleasure?
opts: Natural pleasures become harmful
The drug blocks all sensation
The senses stop sending information
The brain can no longer evaluate the information as pleasure
questions.why: Detail: 'Information … still reaches the brain, but the brain is unable to evaluate and interpret it as pleasure'. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Legal Officer), Sep 2023.

questions.q: In contrast to drug-induced pleasure, natural pleasures
opts: enlarge satisfaction and can be repeated indefinitely
disturb mental processes
weaken the pleasure reflexes
are artificially stimulated
questions.why: Detail: the last sentence. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Legal Officer), Sep 2023.

questions.q: The tone of the passage is best described as
opts: explanatory and cautionary
humorous
indifferent
nostalgic
questions.why: Tone: it explains a mechanism and warns of harm. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Legal Officer), Sep 2023.
